criterion_notes.c1: No. Although the constitutional debates and statutory frameworks reviewed topically concern people's access to pipeline water, the study explicitly excludes local-level water access efforts and empirically examines national-level legislative/constitutional reform processes rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2, but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines legal, institutional, regulatory, and governance factors (constitutional ESCR provisions, national water and privatization statutes, regulatory bodies, and judicial writs such as tutela and amparo). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, however, these macro-level legal opportunity structures are analyzed only as political/institutional determinants of whether Congresses pass constitutional amendments, not as rule-type mechanisms (e.g., eligibility rules, documentation/tenure, tariffs, enforcement, or utility structure) directly governing household or community service access. Note that plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper also fails Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 (no empirical service-access outcome).
criterion_notes.c3: Yes (for political/legislative analysis, though without empirical service-access data). Section 3 reports a comparative qualitative content analysis of 3 constitutions, 12 laws, 5 regulatory rules, 21 constitutional bills, and 2 constitutional court rulings across Brazil, Colombia, and Peru, supplemented by confidential interviews noted in the IRB and Data Availability statements.
criterion_notes.c4: No. The dependent variable / outcome analyzed and reported is national constitutional reform success (approval of Peru's 2017 constitutional amendment versus non-approval of constitutional bills in Brazil and Colombia). The paper reports no empirical outcome measuring household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes for the paper's own comparative national design: unit of analysis (three national jurisdictions / 21 constitutional bills), exposure (domestic legal opportunity structures and political costs), outcome (legislative approval or rejection of constitutional right-to-water amendments), and study design (comparative legal-political case study with document content analysis) are identifiable, though respondent and sample details for the auxiliary interviews noted in the IRB/Data Availability statements are omitted and no household/community population or access outcome is studied.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: In this paper we compare recent efforts towards the constitutionalization of the right to water in Brazil, Colombia, and Peru to understand the opportunities and limitations related to the attempts to enhance access to piped water to the highest normative level.

We acknowledge that there have been important efforts towards the protection of access to pipeline water at the local level, but we have not included them in this study because we are focusing on the interaction between domestic legislation at the national level.
We explore the role of the existing domestic legal frameworks on drinkable water provision and water management towards the approval of constitutional amendments.

Overall, we analyzed each country’s constitution, 12 laws, 5 regulatory rules, 21 constitutional bills, 2 constitutional court rulings, and made a broad analysis of constitutional case law trends based on secondary literature.
We argue that legal opportunity structures build legal environments that influence constitutional reform success.
While Peru passed a constitutional reform establishing a freestanding constitutional right to water in 2017, similar efforts in Brazil and Colombia have proven unsuccessful.

raw_response.exposure: Domestic legal opportunity structures (pre-existing constitutional protection of socio-economic rights, statutory drinking-water and privatization frameworks, and judicial enforcement mechanisms such as tutela and amparo) and political/financial costs of reform
raw_response.outcome: Legislative approval or non-approval of national constitutional amendments enshrining the right to water (no household or community water or sanitation service access outcome reported)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Three national jurisdictions (Brazil, Colombia, and Peru; unit of analysis: country / national constitutional reform process), covering 3 constitutions, 12 laws, 5 regulatory rules, 21 constitutional bills (2010-2019), and 2 constitutional court rulings (plus confidential interviews noted in IRB/Data Availability statements without reported sample size); no household or community population sampled
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome). This comparative legal-political study analyzes why Peru enacted a constitutional amendment enshrining the right to water in 2017 whereas constitutional reform bills in Brazil and Colombia did not pass Congress. Although the study passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (by analyzing national constitutional, statutory, regulatory, and judicial frameworks) while failing the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (as macro-legal opportunity structures are examined as determinants of legislative constitutional reform rather than mechanisms directly governing household/community service access), it is excluded under both readings because its outcome is national constitutional amendment passage/failure rather than any empirical water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome (c4 = no, c1 = no).
raw_response.study_design: Comparative qualitative legal-political case study using content analysis of constitutions, laws, regulatory rules, constitutional bills, and court rulings (with confidential interviews noted in back-matter)
